title: Customer expectations, pre-existing damage and written limits
audience: Stone and terrazzo restoration technicians, estimators and the people who speak to clients about the result of the work
learningOutcomes: Explain the normal variation in natural stone and terrazzo and set client expectations before work starts
Photograph and record pre-existing damage before touching the surface
State the limits of the work in writing, including exclusions and what may remain after the work
Handle a client complaint about the finish through the business escalation route
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: ACCC, Consumer rights and guarantees (services) (published and modified 17 July 2026, per page metadata); DEWR, Prohibition on the use of engineered stone (no date shown).

instruction.heading: Set the expectation before the work starts
instruction.body: Natural stone and terrazzo vary. Colour changes across a slab, veining and fine lines are normal features of the stone, and pits and natural voids are part of the material. Terrazzo has chips of varying colour and size set in a matrix. Restoration changes the sheen and sometimes the colour, and the result depends on the stone, the age of the finish, the wear, the existing sealer and the test patch. Explain this to the client before the work starts, in plain words and in writing. Services under the Australian Consumer Law must be performed with reasonable care and competence, and finished in a timely manner where no time is agreed. Do not promise a mirror finish, a colour match or the removal of a particular mark until the test patch has shown what is achievable. Once the test patch is done, tell the client the result, and record the client's acknowledgement of it.

instruction.heading: Record the damage that was already there
instruction.body: Walk the site with the client before the work starts, and photograph the existing chips, cracks, stains, etch marks, previous repairs, lifting, loose tiles and grout failure. Record each item with its position and the date. Record anything that is outside scope, such as a crack that needs structural repair or a loose tile that needs re-fixing. Pre-existing damage protects both the client and the business: it shows what was there before the work, and it shows which problems the work did not cause. Tell the client in writing where a stain or mark may not be removed by the work. Record the client's acknowledgement with the photographs in the job record.

instruction.heading: Write the limits and handle a complaint
instruction.body: State the limits of the work in writing. The limits include what the business will and will not do, that engineered stone is not taken on by this business (“The engineered stone prohibition and what it means on a job”), that structural repair, cutting and installation are out of scope, and that some marks may remain after the test patch and the work. Keep communication respectful and clear, and do not make legal statements about regulated work that the business is not authorised to give. Privacy and access rules apply to the client's home or premises, and the client's property is handled under the business privacy policy. If the client complains about the finish, record the complaint, check it against the test patch record and the photographs, and follow the complaint escalation route in the business policy. A complaint is not resolved by promising a different finish that the work cannot give.

procedure: Walk the site with the client and agree on the access, the water, the power and the areas to be left out of the work.
Photograph and record the pre-existing damage with its position, date and any out-of-scope items.
Explain the normal variation in the stone and the expected result, based on the assessment and the test patch.
Agree on the scope and exclusions in writing, and record the client's acknowledgement.
After the work, walk the finished surface with the client and record the outcome against the agreed scope.
Give the client the written care note from “Sealing, stain protection and cure times” at handover.
If a complaint is made, record it, check the record, and follow the complaint escalation route.

workedExamples.situation: A client expects a mirror finish on a forty-year-old honed granite floor, which has deep etch marks from a previous cleaning product. The client wants the marks removed in full, and says the quote is cheap for the result.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the technician say, and what should be recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: Deep etch marks may not be removed by honing and polishing, and a mirror finish is not something the test patch has shown. The technician explains that the test patch will show what is possible, carries out the patch, shows the client the result, and records the discussion and the client's acknowledgement in writing. Alternatives are offered, such as a partial removal with a different sheen, or a note that the marks may remain. The technician does not promise the removal and does not use a stronger chemical to force the finish without the test and the client's written approval.

equipmentAndPpe: Camera or phone with date stamp
Client acknowledgement form or electronic signature
Complaint record form and the business escalation contact

commonErrors.error: Promising a finish before the test patch.
commonErrors.prevention: Promise only what the test patch supports, and record what was shown to the client.

commonErrors.error: Not photographing existing chips and cracks before work starts.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the damage before the first pass. A photograph after the work does not show what was there before.
Put the limits and exclusions in the written quote and scope, and get the client's acknowledgement.

commonErrors.error: Answering a complaint by offering a different finish the work cannot give.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the complaint against the test record and photographs, then follow the escalation route.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Client communication must not imply that engineered stone work, or any other regulated work, is lawful for this business. Decline or refer such work in writing (“The engineered stone prohibition and what it means on a job”).
Client privacy, access and property are handled under the business privacy policy and the site induction. This lesson does not change those duties.
Stop-work rule: stop and do not proceed with any work the client has not agreed to in writing, or where the surface identification is not established.

qualityStandard: The client has been told the expected result, in writing, before the work starts.
Pre-existing damage is photographed and recorded with its position and date.
Scope and exclusions are agreed in writing and acknowledged by the client.
Complaints are recorded and followed through the escalation route.
documentationEvidence: Pre-existing damage photograph log with position and date
Client acknowledgement of the expected result and the limits
Complaint record and escalation outcome, where applicable
summary: Set the expected result in writing, and confirm it after the test patch.
Photograph existing damage before the first pass.
State the limits and exclusions in writing.
Do not promise a finish or a regulated outcome the work cannot give.
Handle complaints through the escalation route with the records in hand.
referencesAtEnd: Official sources to recheck before any job: ACCC, Consumer rights and guarantees (services) (published and modified 17 July 2026, per page metadata); DEWR, Prohibition on the use of engineered stone (no date shown).

knowledgeChecks.question: When should the client's expectations about the finish be set?
options: Before the work starts, and confirmed after the test patch
After the job is finished and paid for in full by the client
Only if the client asks about the finish at the start of the job
Never, at any stage of the work, the test patch or the job

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should pre-existing damage be recorded before work starts?
options: To increase the price of the job later on the site, the bill and the total
It documents the starting condition and protects both the client and the business
It is only needed for insurance claims later on the job, the file and the policy
It is not necessary for this kind of job or any stone surface at all

knowledgeChecks.question: A client expects a mirror finish on old honed granite. What is the correct response?
options: Promise the finish, since it is achievable on this old granite and the whole job
Refuse without explanation, since the finish is not possible at all on this job
Explain that the test patch shows what is achievable, and record the discussion
Use acid to force the finish on the stone surface, the edges and the corners

knowledgeChecks.question: Which limit should be written into the scope?
options: That the business will fix all cracks in the stone, the tiles and the grout
That the client may do anything they like to the stone at any time they want
That no records will be kept of the job or the stone at all
That engineered stone is excluded and structural repair is out of scope

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should a client's complaint about a finish be sent first?
options: The business complaint escalation route in the policy
Nowhere, since no complaint route is needed
The regulator for every complaint raised on the job
The client's neighbour, who is nearby and can help
